8. Two loan portfolios both sit on the efficient frontier. Portfolio A has an expected return of 6 per cent and risk of 4 per cent. Portfolio B has an expected return of 9 per cent and risk of 8 per cent. With a risk-free rate of 2 per cent, which has the higher Sharpe ratio?

   ::: {.content-hidden when-meta="include-answers"}
   - [ ] A, because it earns more return per unit of risk
   - [ ] B, because its expected return is higher
   - [ ] They are equal, because both lie on the efficient frontier
   - [ ] It cannot be determined without the correlation between them
   :::
   ::: {.content-hidden unless-meta="include-answers"}
   - [x] A, because it earns more return per unit of risk
   - [ ] B, because its expected return is higher
   - [ ] They are equal, because both lie on the efficient frontier
   - [ ] It cannot be determined without the correlation between them

   *Working:* $S_A=(6-2)/4=1.00$ and $S_B=(9-2)/8=0.875$. The higher return does not win; the higher return **per unit of risk** does.
   :::

# Short answer questions

## Q1

How do loan portfolio risks differ from individual loan risks?

::: {.content-hidden unless-meta="include-answers"}
::: {.callout-tip title="Example answer"}
Loan portfolio risks refer to the risks of a portfolio of loans as opposed to the risks of a single loan. Inherent in the distinction is the elimination of some of the risks of individual loans because of benefits from diversification.
:::
:::

## Q2

Why is it difficult for small banks, credit unions and building societies to measure credit risk using modern portfolio theory?

::: {.content-hidden unless-meta="include-answers"}
::: {.callout-tip title="Example answer"}
The basic premise behind modern portfolio theory is the ability to diversify and reduce risk by eliminating diversifiable risk. Small banks, credit unions and building societies
may not have the ability to diversify their asset base, especially if the local markets in which they serve have a limited number of industries. The ability to diversify is even more acute if these loans cannot be traded easily.
:::
:::

## Q3

CountrySide Bank uses the Moody’s Analytics RiskFrontier model to evaluate the risk–return characteristics of the loans in its portfolio. A specific $10 million loan earns 2 per cent per year in fees, and the loan is priced at a 4 per cent spread over the cost of funds for the bank. For collateral considerations, the loss to the bank if the borrower defaults will be 20 per cent of the loan’s face value. The expected probability of default is 3 per cent. What is the anticipated return on this loan? What is the risk of the loan?

::: {.content-hidden unless-meta="include-answers"}
::: {.callout-tip title="Example answer"}
Expected return is $AIS_i-E(L_i) = (0.02+0.04)-(0.03\times0.2) = 0.054$

Risk of the loan is $\sigma_i = \sqrt{EDF_i(1-EDF_i)} \times LGD_i = \sqrt{0.03\times 0.97} \times 0.2 = 0.0341$, or 3.41%.
:::
:::

## Q4

BOQ's loan book at 31 August 2025 was 74 per cent residential mortgages, spread across tens of thousands of separate borrowers in several states.

(a) An analyst argues that with so many individual borrowers the portfolio must be well diversified. Explain why that reasoning is incomplete.
(b) Suppose each mortgage has a standard deviation of 4 per cent and the average pairwise correlation between them is 0.25. What is the lowest portfolio risk the bank could reach by adding more mortgages of the same kind?
(c) Given your answer to (b), name two things the bank can do about the risk that remains.

::: {.content-hidden unless-meta="include-answers"}
::: {.callout-tip title="Example answer"}
(a) Adding loans only removes the **idiosyncratic** part of the risk, the part specific to one borrower. Every mortgage in the book responds to the same underlying drivers: unemployment, interest rates and house prices. That shared exposure makes them positively correlated, and correlation puts a floor under portfolio risk that no amount of extra lending can break through. Counting borrowers measures the wrong thing; what matters is how many distinct *risk factors* the book is exposed to.

(b) For an equally weighted portfolio of $N$ loans with common correlation $\rho$,

$$\sigma_p = \sigma\sqrt{\frac{1}{N} + \left(1-\frac{1}{N}\right)\rho} \;\xrightarrow[N\to\infty]{}\; \sigma\sqrt{\rho}$$

So the floor is $4\% \times \sqrt{0.25} = \mathbf{2\%}$. Risk falls from 4 per cent on a single loan to at best 2 per cent, and never to zero.

(c) Any two of: **hold capital** against the undiversifiable part; **sell or hedge it**, for example through RMBS securitisation, lenders mortgage insurance, or credit derivatives; or **change the mix** by lending into genuinely different risk factors rather than more of the same.
:::
:::

## Q5

How is selling a credit forward similar to buying a put option?

::: {.content-hidden unless-meta="include-answers"}
::: {.callout-tip title="Example answer"}
After the loan is made, the FI sells a credit forward. If the credit quality of the borrower deteriorates sufficiently that the spread over the benchmark bond increases, the forward seller (the FI) will realise a gain at the maturity of the forward contract that will offset the decrease in value of the loan. Thus, the FI is compensated as the borrower's credit quality deteriorates. This is the exact same situation as a put option buyer when the stock price goes down.

If the credit quality improves, the lender FI will pay the forward buyer because the benchmark spread will have decreased. However, since the spread can only decrease to zero, the FI has limited loss exposure. This is similar to paying a premium on a put option.

Note: sign conventions for credit forwards differ across texts. See the lecture's footnote on credit spread forwards.
:::
:::
